newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - U.S. markets take Lebed ouster in stride.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - U.S. markets take Lebed ouster in stride.

text.p: The ouster of Russian security chief Alexander Lebed sent mild shivers through U.S. financial markets on Thursday, but experts said any sustained moves will require clearer signals about the Russian political outlook.
For investors, the key question remains who would come into power if President Boris Yeltsin were to step down or was no longer able to fulfill his presidential duties.
The terms of the succession struggle were certainly altered by the news of Lebed's sacking, but not in the clear-cut manner that markets crave.

"What (Lebed's ouster) does is take what has already been a messy and rather intense struggle for succession and it will not mitigate it in any fashion, but simply change its terms," said Robert Legvold, a professor at Columbia University's Harriman Institute.

For the markets, this ambiguity translated into a sharp but seemingly fleeting reaction. Rumors of Yeltsin's poor health have prompted a knee-jerk ripple effect in U.S. markets in recent weeks and news of Lebed's sacking had much the same impact.
The dollar surged to a 4-1/2-month high of 1.5454 marks in the aftermath of the news, before paring gains to trade near 1.5430 around midday.

"It was a reason to buy dollars, but I don't think it's a reason for sustained dollar strength by any means, and I wouldn't be surprised to see a slip back to where we were before this thing happened," said Earl Johnson, foreign exchange economist at the Bank of Montreal.
Dollar-denominated Russian Vneshekonombank loans fell as much as 2-1/2 points immediately following the announcement of Lebed's firing before rebounding to trade down 1-3/4 points.

Oil prices meanwhile, were higher across the board, but analysts said the oil market's attention was elsewhere, with the focus remaining on the short supply of heating oil in the U.S. and Europe ahead of winter.
The Lebed sacking "certainly has the potential to be disruptive, but I don't really think it has that much significance yet," said Jack McIntyre, energy analyst at McCarthy Crisanti Maffei.
The Russian oil industry has only recently stabilized after years of decline, but oil exports have continued to flow despite various large scale upheavals over the past decade.
"When, or ... if, the Russian oil industry ever really lives up to its potential, that is when it will have a big impact (on the world oil market)," said McIntyre.
Rating agency Standard & Poor's underscored the muted reaction to Lebed's ouster on Thursday when it announced it would stick by its BB-minus Russian foreign currency rating.

"If something like that would affect our rating then our rating would be worth nothing," said Helena Hessel, director of S&P's sovereign ratings group. "Our rating is not based on whether Lebed is security chief or not."

However, experts said the markets will keep a close eye on Russian political developments in the months to come. Yeltsin is scheduled to undergo heart surgery in mid-November and the succession battle is likely to heat up.
"The others within the government will continue to fight one another and Lebed will now become a focal point for opposition on the outside," said Columbia University's Legvold.
Other contenders for power include Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov, current Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and to a lesser extent Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov.
Powerful, but politically unpopular, chief of staff Anatoly Chubais, an ardent free market advocate, is also considered a key player within the Kremlin.
Legvold said Lebed's sacking would clearly impede his coalition-building capabilities within the government and diminish his public role on a global basis.
He noted, however, that these disadvantages would be partly offset by a newfound freedom to lobby publicly for the presidency.
